## **Introduction**

CArp is an app I developed with the assistance of ChatGPT and Claude.  It is based on an earlier program I wrote myself using Supercollider.  

The purpose of CArp is to produce MIDI output based on the resultants of interference between different lists of serial parameters.  The inspiration for this was my work with the Schillinger System of Musical Composition where this is a foundational means of generating extensive musical variety from relatively simple starting material.  

As a simple example to illustrate what I'm talking about, consider that if you had a pitch sequence of three notes and superimposed that on a series of note durations that was four notes long, you would end up with a final musical phrase that is twelve notes long.

Obviously this is a very simple example.  You can imagine how complex the final output becomes when synchronizing larger series and more than two musical parameters.    
CArp is divided into four pages:  **Melody, Chords, Bass,** and **Percussion**.  By default, they operate independently, but you can optionally have Melody, Chords, and Bass interact with one another.  

## **Basic Behavior**

Each page has a number of modules composed of a series of elements (cells).  These series each loop *independently* and *indefinitely*.  When you click **Play**, the first element of each series is evaluated before proceeding on to the next.  The final output on that page at any given moment is the combined effect of all of those series.  As you will see, this includes:  the notes you have chosen, the order that those notes should be played, the rhythmic duration of those notes, variable transposition of those notes, and their geometric inversion state.  

At the top of each page you will see the following:

- **Channel**:  the MIDI channel that this page outputs to.   
- **Octave**:  select overall final octave transposition for the whole page.   
- **Velocity**:  lets you scale the velocity of the output notes. 

## **Melody (and Bass)**

The first module is **Notes**, which is where you will enter the pitches you plan to work with.  

- You can double-click in a cell to type in the note name or you can change it by clicking and dragging up or down.    
- To add or remove cells, click the **\+** or **\-** buttons.  These buttons add or remove from the end of the series, but you can delete other cells by option-clicking it, and you can re-order the cells by holding command and dragging it.    
- The **rev** button reverses (retrogrades) the series  
- **\<\<** and **\>\>** permutate the series left or right.  When shifting left, the initial value moves to the end, and when shifting right, the end value moves to the beginning.  This is what Schillinger calls “circular permutation.”  


The next module is **Order**, where you set the order that you will play back the pitches in **Notes**.  In a sense, this is actually where the melody lives.  When starting out, it would be tempting to input all the pitches of your melody in their proper order into **Notes**, but this is actually less efficient than simply using **Notes** as the total collection of pitches you wish to work with and using **Order** to write the sequence itself.  

- For convenience, there is an **auto** button, which automatically generates a new row with sequential values from 1 to N, where N \= the number of elements in **Notes**.    
- **Add row** and **remove row** do what you’d expect them to.  
- When there is more than one row, you can click the little circle to the right of the row and drag to re-order the rows.    
- **Copy** simply duplicates the last row as a new row.  

**Rhythm** is the duration of each note.  There is a drop-down menu for the time-unit, and each cell is a multiple of this time unit.  So if you choose ⅛ for the t-unit and you have a rhythmic sequence of 3, 3, 2, this means you have dotted ⅛, dotted ⅛, ¼ (calculated from 3 x ⅛, 3 x ⅛, 2 x ⅛).  

The **Rests** series determines whether the current rhythmic duration will actually be played or whether it will be a rest of that value.  “Eat note” determines whether the current note value will be passed over for this rest or if it will be picked up on the next non-rested rhythmic value.  

**Transpose** determines the current state of transposition.  Values indicate semitones, and can be positive or negative.  

**Transpose Rhythm** determines the length of time that the active transposition value is used.  

**Inverse** will flip the active note(s) around a particular pitch axis.  For instance, if the current note is D4 and you have a pitch axis of C4, the output will be Bb3.  This is because D4 is two semitones above C4, but **Inverse** flips this relationship upside down so that the actual note played is two semitones below instead.  

**Inverse Rhythm** determines the length of time that the active inversion state is used.  

The **Bass** page works essentially the same as **Melody.**

## **Chords**

As you can see, this page has mostly all the same modules as **Melody**, with a couple of important differences.  

- **Chords** differs from **Notes** in that each row here represents pitches that will be played simultaneously.    
- **Order** determines the order of the above *rows*, not the order of elements within those rows.  Again, there is an **auto** button at the end which will generate a row with elements 1 \- N, where N \= the number of chords (i.e. the number of rows in the **Chords** module).    
- **Change** is the harmonic rhythm, i.e. the duration that each chord is active.    
- **Rhythm** determines the way the chords are actually played.  Pay attention to the distinction here:  whereas in **Melody** each rhythmic value plays one note at which point both **Rhythm** and **Order** move on to their next term, **Rhythm** in the **Chords** page does not increment the current chord \- that’s **Change**’s job.  This might sound complicated, but I think you’ll find that it’s fairly intuitive once you start using it. 




## **Percussion**

This page is a little bit different than the others.  It is nowhere near as “deep,” and is mostly intended just to provide some rudimentary accompaniment, but does allow for some interesting creativity that typical drum machines don’t afford you, such as independent loop length for different elements of the “kit.”  

Instead of modules we now have **Parts**.  Which each have:

- A MIDI note selector which determines what note that part uses.  Common values would be C2 for kick, D2 for snare, Ab2 for closed hi-hat, Bb2 for open hi-hat, etc.    
- The cells here look more like a typical drum sequencer where each cell is either on (marked with an **X**) or off (empty).    
- **\-8** and **\+8** allow for quick creation of a bunch of cells so you don’t have to click \- and \+ a lot of times.


At the top of the page are also a couple of features unique to this page:

- **Tempo**:  You can easily select to have this page obey the tempo set in the BPM field or play at double- or half-time relative to that.    
- **Gate**:  this determines the actual length of the output MIDI notes.  This is advantageous so that if your t-values in this page are longer (like ¼) and you record to your DAW or sequencer, you won’t end up with long notes.    

## Modes

You may have noticed the **Modes** drop-down menu in the upper right.  This is where things get particularly interesting.  This is where you set how the first three pages interact with one another.  

By default, you will see M H B.  This indicates that each page, Melody, Harmony (Chords), and Bass determine their own **Notes.**  But let’s say you wanted to have **Chords** generate its own notes but **Melody** to derive its notes from the active chord.  

When you select M \<- H  B and open the **Melody** page, you will notice that **Notes** is no longer a list of notes but a list of chord tones.  Everything else on this page has stayed the same, but now each note is an index of whatever chord is currently playing.  Note that **Order** is still in charge here.  **Chord tone(s)** should still be thought of as the collection of tones that this page works with.  

Now let’s say you wanted to program a **Melody** but you want the chords to harmonize those notes.  If you choose M \-\> H  B, **Chords** no longer contains note names.  (*Note that this configuration is somewhat more experimental and is probably the feature of CArp that is most likely to be adjusted in the future).*  

In this configuration, **Chords** is now a list of pitch integers, which will be familiar to anyone who has worked with PC sets and serialist music.  For example, 0 4 7 is the integer form of a major chord:  0 \= root, 4 \= four semitones above (i.e. major third), and 7 \= seven semitones up (i.e. perfect fifth).  Please read the following carefully to understand how this is actually used. 

At the beginning of a new **Change**, each chord immediately looks at whatever note is starting in **Melody** and sets itself such that *the final element in the current chord will be equal to that note.*  For example, let’s say the melody note is B4, and the integer notation for the new chord is 0 4 7 11\.  If 11 \= B4, then 0 \= C4, 4 \= E4, 7 \= G4.  So the current chord (for the entire duration of this **Change** is a Cmaj7 chord, i.e. C E G B.  Remember that, for the sake of the chord being played, the order of the notes in the chord row don’t matter.  They only matter for which note is intended to match the melody.  In other words, let’s say you had the exact same integer notation for the chord but in a different order:  11 4 7 0\.  That same melody note, B4, will still trigger a major7 chord because the tones have not changed.  But B4 now \= 0\.  4 \= D\#, 7 \= F\#, and 11 \= A\#.  This might sound complicated but as a general workflow tip, just do the following:  write whatever integer notation you want for the chosen chord type you want, and then just move the tone you want to match the melody to the end.  If you want the melody to match the root, move 0 (or 12\) to the end.  

## **Set-up, etc.**

You can use CArp with any MIDI device (accessible with the MIDI Out menu at the top).  I suspect that probably the way that most people will use this is with a DAW.  On Mac the easiest way to do this is by using the IAC Driver bus (in Audio MIDI Setup).  

Currently there is no host sync.  That will probably be added at some point.  

Please note that while you can theoretically make full songs in CArp, its main intended purpose is to generate ideas and thematic variation.  The evolution of what it generates is as complex as you want to make it.  You can use it to make simple loops or more unpredictable generative music.  This is a bit of a different approach to generative music \- it is entirely deterministic.  If you press stop and play again, you will get the exact same piece of music as before.  While most generative systems rely on some random elements as their main source of variation and unpredictability, with CArp the results are in theory 100% predictable, but due to the number of variables involved, it is unlikely that you will know *exactly* what it’s going to do once you start involving several modules using series that are of different lengths.  This is a big part (although by no means the entirety) of what gives the Schillinger System of Musical Composition its incredible utility as a means of generating novel musical material.
